definition: Loading data in scheduled, finite chunks — hourly/daily jobs that move a bounded set each run.
explanation: A batch job extracts a slice (e.g. yesterday's orders) and loads it on a schedule. Simple to reason about and retry, but data is only as fresh as the interval. The default for warehouse/reporting pipelines.
interviewLine: Batch ingestion moves bounded data on a schedule — simple and retryable, but only as fresh as its interval.
whyItMatters: Most analytics pipelines are batch; knowing when it's enough avoids needless streaming complexity.

definition: Continuously ingesting events as they occur, via a broker like Kafka, for low-latency freshness.
explanation: Instead of scheduled pulls, producers push events to a log and consumers land them continuously. Enables real-time dashboards and alerting, but adds ordering, delivery-semantics, and state concerns batch avoids.
interviewLine: Streaming ingestion lands events continuously through a broker for freshness, at the cost of ordering and delivery-semantics complexity.
whyItMatters: It's the ingestion side of any real-time use case — the alternative when hourly batches are too stale.

definition: Full load re-copies the entire source each run; incremental moves only rows changed since last run.
explanation: Full loads are simple and self-healing but expensive and slow at scale. Incremental loads track a high-water mark (updated_at/id) and fetch only newer rows — fast and cheap, but must handle deletes and late updates carefully.
interviewLine: Full loads recopy everything (simple, costly); incremental moves only changed rows via a high-water mark (cheap, but must handle deletes/late data).
whyItMatters: Picking incremental correctly is what keeps large pipelines affordable without dropping data.
commonMistake: Incremental on updated_at while ignoring hard deletes — deleted source rows silently persist in the target.

definition: Capturing every insert/update/delete from a source database as a stream of change events.
explanation: Instead of polling for changed rows, CDC reads the database's transaction log (WAL/binlog) to emit each change in order — including deletes. It's low-impact on the source and gives near-real-time, complete replication.
interviewLine: CDC streams every insert/update/delete by reading the DB transaction log, capturing deletes and order without polling the source.
whyItMatters: Log-based CDC is the modern standard for syncing operational databases into the warehouse/lake.
interviewQuestion: Why is log-based CDC preferred over query-based (timestamp polling) CDC?

definition: An open-source, log-based CDC platform that streams database changes into Kafka.
explanation: Debezium connectors tail the WAL/binlog of Postgres, MySQL, Mongo, etc., and publish ordered change events to Kafka topics with before/after images. It's the common engine behind real-time DB-to-lake pipelines.
interviewLine: Debezium is log-based CDC that tails a database's binlog/WAL and emits ordered before/after change events to Kafka.
whyItMatters: It's the reference implementation interviewers expect you to name for log-based CDC.

definition: The stored marker (max timestamp or id) of the last successfully ingested record, used to resume.
explanation: Each incremental run reads rows greater than the stored high-water mark, processes them, then advances the mark. It makes loads resumable and avoids reprocessing — but a too-coarse mark can skip rows written out of order.
interviewLine: A high-water mark records the last-ingested position (max id/timestamp) so the next run reads only newer rows and can resume after failure.
whyItMatters: The high-water mark is the tiny piece of state that makes incremental ingestion correct and restartable.
commonMistake: Advancing the mark before the load commits — a mid-load crash then skips the rows you never wrote.

definition: Designing loads so re-running them produces the same result — safe retries with no duplicates.
explanation: Because jobs fail and retry, ingestion must be replay-safe: use upserts on a key, deterministic partitions you can overwrite, or dedup on a unique event id. Then 'run it again' is always safe.
interviewLine: Idempotent ingestion makes re-runs safe — via keyed upserts, overwritable partitions, or dedup — so retries never create duplicates.
whyItMatters: Idempotency is what lets you retry or backfill without corrupting the target with duplicates.
interviewQuestion: How would you make an append-only pipeline idempotent under retries?

definition: Loading historical data into a pipeline built for going-forward data — filling the gap before it existed.
explanation: When you add a source or fix a bug, you replay past periods to populate history. Backfills must be idempotent and partition-scoped so you can rerun a date range without touching or duplicating other data.
interviewLine: Backfilling replays historical partitions into a pipeline; it relies on idempotent, partition-scoped loads so reruns don't duplicate data.
whyItMatters: Every real pipeline needs a backfill eventually; doing it without double-counting requires idempotent design.
commonMistake: Backfilling into an append-only sink and doubling every row that already loaded.

definition: Handling source schema changes — added, removed, or retyped columns — without breaking the pipeline.
explanation: Sources drift: a new column appears, a type changes. Robust ingestion detects drift and applies a policy — add new columns automatically, reject incompatible type changes, and version the schema (often via a registry) so consumers aren't surprised.
interviewLine: Schema evolution manages source drift with a policy — auto-add columns, block breaking type changes — often enforced via a schema registry.
whyItMatters: Unhandled schema drift is a top cause of overnight pipeline breakages.
interviewQuestion: Which schema changes are backward-compatible, and which force a consumer update?

definition: Pulling data from REST/GraphQL APIs, handling pagination, rate limits, retries, and auth.
explanation: API sources cap page size and requests/min. You page through cursors, respect 429/Retry-After with backoff, refresh tokens, and checkpoint progress so a mid-pull failure resumes rather than restarts.
interviewLine: API ingestion pages through cursors within rate limits, backing off on 429s and checkpointing progress so partial pulls resume cleanly.
whyItMatters: SaaS data (Stripe, Salesforce) mostly arrives via APIs; robust paging and rate handling is the daily grind.
commonMistake: Ignoring Retry-After and hammering a rate-limited API until it bans the client.

definition: Ingesting files dropped into a landing zone (S3/GCS) — CSV, JSON, Parquet — often event-triggered.
explanation: Producers land files in a bucket; ingestion lists new files (or reacts to an object-created event), parses them, and loads them, then archives or marks them processed so they aren't picked up twice.
interviewLine: File ingestion consumes files from a landing zone, tracking processed files (or reacting to object events) so each loads exactly once.
whyItMatters: Landing-zone file drops remain one of the most common integration patterns across enterprises.

definition: Managed connectors (Fivetran, Airbyte) that extract from sources and load raw data into the warehouse.
explanation: Rather than hand-code every connector, these tools offer prebuilt source integrations, incremental sync, schema-drift handling, and CDC — landing raw data for dbt to transform. Buy-vs-build tilts toward buy for the long tail of SaaS sources.
interviewLine: ELT tools like Fivetran/Airbyte provide managed connectors that extract and load raw data incrementally, leaving transformation to dbt.
whyItMatters: They're the 'E' and 'L' of the modern ELT stack, freeing teams to focus on the 'T'.

definition: A side channel where records that fail processing are parked instead of blocking or being lost.
explanation: When a message can't be parsed or violates a rule, routing it to a dead-letter queue keeps the main pipeline flowing while preserving the bad record for inspection, alerting, and later replay after a fix.
interviewLine: A dead-letter queue parks unprocessable records so the pipeline keeps flowing and bad data can be inspected and replayed after a fix.
whyItMatters: DLQs are how you avoid the choice between a stuck pipeline and silently dropped data.

definition: Removing duplicate records at load time — via upserts on a key or filtering on a unique event id.
explanation: At-least-once sources and retries deliver duplicates. Dedup uses a MERGE/upsert on a natural or event key, or windowed dedup on an id, so the target holds one row per logical event regardless of redelivery.
interviewLine: Ingest dedup collapses redelivered records via keyed upserts or unique-id filtering, so at-least-once sources don't double-count.
whyItMatters: Without dedup, at-least-once delivery inflates every count and metric downstream.
interviewQuestion: How do you dedup an unbounded stream without unbounded state?
